steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening, Magnus climbed 127 steps.

He'd counted them so many times the number had lost meaning, become just a rhythm his legs followed while his mind wandered elsewhere — to his daughter in the city, to the letter he kept meaning to write, to the particular gray the ocean turned before a storm.

Tonight the storm came fast.

By eight o'clock the wind was pulling at the tower like something that wanted in. Rain moved sideways past the glass. Magnus kept the light turning and watched the dark water the way a doctor watches a patient — looking for what he hoped not to find.

He found it anyway.

A shape. Low and wrong against the waves.

He grabbed his radio, his coat, his boots. He was sixty-three years old with one good knee and no business running down a wet hill in the dark, but he ran.

The boat had four people in it. A family, it turned out — parents and two children, sailing back from a holiday, caught off guard by the speed of it all. He pulled them up the rocks one by one, talking the whole time about nothing, just so they could follow the sound of his voice.

Later, wrapped in his blankets, drinking his tea, the youngest child — a girl of maybe seven — looked up at the light still turning overhead.

"Do you get lonely up there?" she asked.

Magnus thought about it honestly.

"Not on nights like this," he said.
